title: Non-Linear Matrix Self-Adaptive Aggregation Learning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to matrix aggregation, termed Non-Linear Matrix Self-Adaptive Aggregation Learning (NLMAAL), designed to enhance the generalization capabilities of machine learning models. Traditional aggregation methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting the model's ability to adapt to complex data patterns. NLMAAL dynamically adjusts aggregation weights based on the data's inherent non-linear relationships, enabling the model to automatically learn and optimize its representation. The paper details the core mechanisms of the method, including a dynamic weighting scheme and a novel optimization strategy to mitigate the limitations of fixed parameter approaches. We demonstrate the effectiveness of NLMAAL through extensive experimentation on several benchmark datasets, showcasing significant improvements in model performance and robustness.

title: Probability Field Simulation for Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probabilistic field simulation approach designed to enhance quantum computing by leveraging its inherent advantages and utilizing parallel computation to accelerate algorithm validation and optimization. Traditional quantum computing demands extreme precision, while probability field simulation offers a pathway to significantly reduced computational complexity. The core mechanism involves approximating quantum computation through a probabilistic framework, effectively utilizing parallel computation to expedite the verification and refinement of quantum algorithms. This work presents a framework for efficient quantum algorithm design and validation, demonstrating the potential for significantly improved computational performance. The paper provides a detailed explanation of the methodology, showcasing its benefits and limitations.

title: Title: Bayesian Constraint Optimization for Quantum Field Theory
abstract: This paper explores the application of Bayesian Constraint Optimization (BCO) to quantum field theory simulations. Traditional parameter tuning methods often rely on trial-and-error, which can be computationally expensive and may not accurately capture the underlying physics. We propose a novel Bayesian framework leveraging a dynamically adjusted Bayesian network to intelligently prioritize energy stability and coherence – key aspects of quantum field theory. The core mechanism involves a 'Adaptive Bayesian Network' that learns the field's dynamics through observation, effectively addressing the inherent uncertainty in complex quantum systems. This approach aims to provide more accurate simulations and accelerate optimization processes compared to conventional methods. The paper details the architecture of the Bayesian network, the learning process, and the resulting performance improvements, demonstrating the efficacy of the BCO framework in simulating fundamental quantum phenomena. The research focuses on a specific example of simulating the Klein-Gordon field, providing a concrete illustration of the methodology's potential.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel data compression algorithm based on quantum topology. Traditional data compression techniques rely on classical algorithms, while this research leverages the unique properties of quantum topology to significantly enhance compression efficiency and algorithm robustness. The core mechanism involves exploiting quantum states to optimize the compression process, resulting in improved data compression rates and enhanced resilience against perturbations. This work explores the potential of quantum topology for data compression and lays the groundwork for future advancements in this field.

title: Quantum-Inspired Optimization of Deep Learning Hyperparameters via Tensor Networks
abstract: Optimizing hyperparameters in deep learning models remains a significant bottleneck in the development and deployment of effective neural networks. Traditional methods, such as grid search and random search, often struggle with the exponentially growing search space, leading to substantial computational costs and limited exploration of potentially optimal configurations. This paper proposes a novel approach to deep learning hyperparameter optimization that leverages the principles of quantum-inspired optimization, specifically employing tensor network methods, notably Matrix Product States (MPS), to efficiently approximate the complex optimization landscape. Our method utilizes quantum-inspired sampling techniques to guide the exploration, effectively mimicking the probabilistic nature of quantum measurements. We demonstrate the feasibility and potential advantages of this approach through theoretical analysis and a conceptual framework. The core of our method lies in representing the hyperparameter space as a tensor network, allowing for efficient calculations of the objective function (e.g., validation loss) without exhaustively evaluating every possible combination. This significantly reduces the computational burden compared to conventional methods. The paper outlines a detailed algorithm and discusses key considerations for implementation, including tensor network construction, sampling strategies, and convergence criteria. We propose a framework for iteratively refining the tensor network representation based on observed validation performance, ultimately converging towards a high-performing hyperparameter configuration. The theoretical underpinning draws upon concepts from quantum mechanics, particularly the idea of measurement and probability distribution, to drive the optimization process. We believe this quantum-inspired approach offers a promising avenue for accelerating deep learning hyperparameter tuning and achieving state-of-the-art performance.

title: Temporal Graph Embedding via Relational Diffusion
abstract: Graph embeddings have emerged as a powerful technique for representing graphs in a continuous vector space, facilitating downstream tasks such as node classification, link prediction, and graph clustering. However, conventional graph embedding methods often treat graph relationships as static, failing to capture the dynamic evolution of these relationships over time. This paper introduces a novel approach, Temporal Graph Embedding via Relational Diffusion, which addresses this limitation by explicitly modeling the temporal dynamics of graph relationships. We leverage a recurrent neural network (RNN) to learn a "diffusion" process across the graph, where node states are iteratively updated based on the states of their neighbors, weighted by learned relational similarity. This process generates a temporal graph embedding where each node is represented by its evolving state vector. The core of our method lies in the integration of relational information within the RNN's recurrent computations, allowing the model to adapt to changes in the graph's structure over time. We demonstrate through theoretical analysis and a conceptual outline that our approach provides a more nuanced representation of graph data, potentially leading to significant improvements in graph-related tasks that require understanding temporal dependencies. This work lays the foundation for future research exploring more sophisticated temporal graph embedding techniques.

title: 基于量子纠缠的非局域性建模与优化
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, offers a potentially transformative approach to modeling and optimization. This paper explores the application of entanglement principles to construct a novel non-local modeling framework, focusing on leveraging entanglement's inherent properties to enhance optimization processes. We propose a mechanism that translates complex problems into entangled states, enabling efficient transformation and potentially unlocking novel solutions. The core claim posits that this framework significantly improves the performance of optimization algorithms, particularly in scenarios where classical methods struggle. This work presents a conceptual foundation for future research and development in leveraging entanglement for advanced optimization techniques.

title: Differential Privacy for Training Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for learning representations from graph-structured data, finding applications in diverse domains like social network analysis, drug discovery, and recommendation systems. However, training GNNs often requires access to sensitive data, raising significant privacy concerns. This work introduces a novel differential privacy mechanism specifically designed for training GNNs. Our approach adds calibrated noise to the gradients during the training process, providing a quantifiable level of privacy protection while maintaining the network's ability to learn effective graph representations. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this method through theoretical analysis and conceptual design. The core claim of this work is to develop a differential privacy mechanism that protects the privacy of the training data while still allowing graph neural networks to learn effective representations. The core mechanism involves adding noise to the gradients during the training process, carefully calibrating the noise level to balance privacy and utility. This addresses the privacy challenges of training GNNs.

title: Title: Adaptive Topology for Data Compression – Quantum-Inspired Algorithms
abstract: This paper investigates the application of adaptive topology in data compression, inspired by the principles of quantum mechanics, to achieve significantly higher compression rates than conventional methods. Traditional compression algorithms rely on static mapping and iterative compression. We propose a novel approach that dynamically adjusts the topology of data structures, identifying and exploiting patterns that maximize information density, leveraging quantum-inspired algorithms to achieve this optimization. The core mechanism involves utilizing quantum algorithms to subtly modify the underlying structure of data representations, leading to a more efficient compression process. The paper details the theoretical framework for this adaptive topology, explores the implementation challenges, and presents initial results demonstrating the potential for substantial compression gains. We argue that this approach represents a significant step toward quantum-inspired data compression, offering a pathway to unprecedented compression efficiency.

title: Self-Healing Neural Networks via Causal Bayesian Network-Based Diagnostics
abstract: Neural networks have demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, yet their inherent fragility and susceptibility to unexpected failures remain a significant challenge. Traditional approaches to neural network failure diagnosis often rely on reactive methods – detecting and correcting errors after they occur. This paper proposes a novel approach to self-healing neural networks by integrating a causal Bayesian network (CBN) to monitor the network's internal state and perform diagnostics. The core idea is to leverage causal relationships between network parameters and observed performance degradation to proactively identify and address potential issues. This approach allows for a deeper understanding of the network's dynamics and enables targeted interventions. Specifically, we develop a framework where the CBN acts as a diagnostic tool, continuously learning and updating its understanding of the network's causal structure. The system identifies causal relationships, enabling the network to adapt its parameters or trigger corrective actions to mitigate performance degradation. This research provides a framework for building more robust and self-healing neural networks.

title: Generative Adversarial Networks for Learning Symbolic Representations
abstract: This paper explores the application of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to the learning of symbolic representations from data. Traditional machine learning approaches often rely on numerical representations, which can struggle to capture the underlying structure and relationships within complex datasets. We propose a novel framework where a GAN is trained to generate symbolic representations – such as logical formulas or mathematical expressions – directly from data. The core of this approach lies in a discriminator that assesses the "symbolic quality" of the generated representations, providing a feedback signal to the generator. This process encourages the generator to produce representations that are not only plausible but also reflect the inherent structure of the data. We argue that this method represents a significant step towards enabling machines to reason and understand concepts in a manner more akin to human cognition. The potential applications span diverse fields, including knowledge representation, automated reasoning, and formal verification.

title: Adaptive Graph Neural Networks with Dynamic Attention Mechanisms
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Adaptive Graph Neural Network (AGNN) architecture designed to address the limitations of traditional Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in dynamic environments. Traditional GNNs typically rely on fixed graph structures and static attention weights, which can lead to suboptimal performance when graphs evolve over time or when node attributes change. The proposed AGNN incorporates dynamic attention mechanisms that adapt to these changes, improving learning efficiency and accuracy. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that monitors graph structure modifications and node attribute updates, dynamically adjusting the attention weights to prioritize relevant neighbors and features. This approach enables the AGNN to effectively capture temporal dependencies and adapt to varying graph topologies, ultimately leading to enhanced performance in tasks such as node classification, link prediction, and graph classification. The experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of the AGNN compared to standard GNNs, highlighting the benefits of dynamic adaptation.

title: Full Bayesian Analysis of ARX Models Under Scale-Mixtures of Normal Errors: An Application to Solar Radiation in Najran, Saudi Arabia
abstract: Autoregressive models with exogenous variables (ARX) constitute a fundamental family of time series tools with broad applicability across engineering, environmental science, and finance. A persistent limitation of standard Bayesian treatments is the Gaussian error assumption, which frequently proves inadequate when dealing with real data displaying heavy tails or occasional extreme observations. To overcome this shortcoming, the present paper develops a complete Bayesian inferential framework for ARX models under the scale-mixtures of normal (SMN) error distribution, integrating model identification, parameter estimation, and multi-step-ahead prediction within a unified scheme. A stochastic search variable selection (SSVS) procedure is adapted to perform simultaneous selection of the autoregressive order and the active exogenous regressors by assigning binary latent indicators to each candidate coefficient. Mixture-of-normals priors are specified for the dynamic and exogenous coefficients and an inverse-gamma prior for the error scale, while Bernoulli priors govern the latent selection indicators. These choices yield tractable full conditional posterior distributions: multivariate normal for the complete coefficient vector, inverse-gamma for the scale, and Bernoulli for the indicators. The conditional predictive distribution of future observations is also multivariate normal. For SMN-specific mixing parameters whose conditionals lack standard forms, Metropolis–Hastings steps are embedded within the Gibbs sampler. An extensive simulation study evaluates recovery accuracy across three SMN distributions and several ARX configurations. The methodology is then applied to the forecasting of daily global horizontal irradiance (GHI) in Najran, southwestern Saudi Arabia, using clear-sky GHI as an exogenous covariate, demonstrating the practical value of the proposed framework in a renewable energy context.

title: SimpleMemVLA: A Simple but Effective Native-Video Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Long-horizon manipulation is partially observable: the information needed to choose the next action may appear only in observations from minutes earlier. Existing memory mechanisms: retrieval banks, learned compressors, recurrent states must decide what to keep from the past before knowing what a future decision will require. This was motivated by the assumption that minute-scale history is too large to process directly, which modern VLM backbones no longer make true. In this work, we introduce SimpleMemVLA, a VLA without a dedicated memory module. It keeps the sampled history intact and passes it to the backbone in the timestamped video format the backbone was pretrained to process; the hidden states of a generated sub-task then form the only channel from history to a standard flow-matching action head. Since consecutive decisions share most of their history, prefilling the shared prefix during action execution keeps latency close to a single-frame VLA. SimpleMemVLA sets a new state of the art on four memory benchmarks without cost on general-purpose control. Holding the backbone and training setup fixed, it outperforms retrieval, compression and recurrent-state mechanisms by a wide margin, and causal interventions confirm that the policy genuinely reads its history. Code available at https://github.com/wadeKeith/SimpleMemVLA

title: Sparse concept attribution for histomorphological hypothesis generation from whole-slide classifiers
abstract: Histology images contain rich morphological information and can provide insights into pathological processes. However, deriving hypotheses relating morphological phenotypes to clinical attributes is bottlenecked by a manual image interpretation step. Here, we demonstrate that this process can be automated through interpretable deep learning. We present SCOPE, a method to interpret slide-level classifiers by combining pathology-specific vision--language models with sparse concept attribution onto a generalist histomorphological concept bank. To measure whether such explanations recover known morphology, we introduce MorphoRecoveryBench, a benchmark of seven tasks with pathologist-curated reference descriptions. On this benchmark, dense concept attribution is indistinguishable from a random baseline, whereas sparse attribution recovers substantial known morphology; decomposing the pooled slide embedding reaches similar explanation correctness at a fraction of the computational cost. Post-hoc interpretation of whole-slide classifiers can thus generate morphological hypotheses at scale, for expert validation.

title: The Import Tax: A Longitudinal Measurement of Startup Cost in the Python Ecosystem
abstract: Companion dataset to "The Import Tax: A Longitudinal Measurement of Startup Cost in the Python Ecosystem" (revised version under review at Software: Practice and Experience; preprint arXiv:2609.02753). It contains every measurement used in the paper, the -X importtime traces, the measurement harness, and the analysis scripts that regenerate every number and figure. What was measured: the import time of the 500 most-downloaded PyPI packages, every quarterly release since 2021Q3, on CPython 3.9 to 3.14 (python-build-standalone builds), on two platforms (Apple M5 / macOS and Intel Xeon E5-2665 / Linux): 33,408 cells per platform, plus the release histories of 65 distributions that live beneath shared namespaces, and the targeted experiments of the revision (dependency-resolution drift under sweep-date and release-era dependencies, hidden submodule cost with usage weighting, cold-start decomposition including a macOS first-load experiment, and the global lazy mode of CPython 3.15). Files: import-tax-dataset.tar.gz holds README.md (data dictionary and provenance), raw/ (all measurement records as gzipped JSONL), analysis-view/ (the matrix with unit-of-analysis annotations), code/ (harness, analysis and Slurm scripts) and SHA256SUMS; the -X importtime traces are nine separate files traces- .tar.gz (place them under import-tax-dataset/traces/ as .tar.gz). title: Federated LoRA Adaptation of BiomedCLIP Across Four International Chest X-Ray Cohorts
abstract: Federated learning (FL) lets institutions train a shared model without exchanging data, and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) makes this practical at scale by communicating only compact low-rank updates. Biomedical imaging is a compelling setting for this combination: patient data are archived behind privacy regulations, and institutions differ widely in scanners, protocols, and compute. Such heterogeneity raises the question of how federated LoRA updates should be aggregated, increasingly pressing as multimodal vision-language models become central to medical image analysis. We benchmark federated Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of BiomedCLIP for chest radiograph classification across four public cohorts on three continents (USA, Vietnam, Spain). Federated LoRA adaptation improves shared-class AUC on all four cohorts over the unadapted BiomedCLIP backbone (mean 0.687 to 0.802), showing that the gains come from federated adaptation rather than from the pretrained model's zero-shot ability. Relative to isolated single-cohort training, federation improves the weaker cohorts while largely preserving the strongest and approaches a centralized reference (0.812) that pools all data. The singular value decomposition (SVD)-based product-space aggregation introduced by FlexLoRA is essential to this gain (naive factor averaging drops mean AUC by 0.097), whereas a drift-correcting optimizer (FedProx) shows no benefit over FedAvg in our single-seed runs, consistent with LoRA's low-rank updates already limiting client drift. Biomedical vision-language models can thus be adapted collaboratively across heterogeneous, geographically distributed institutions without centralizing data.

title: Humanoid Safe Stop via Learned Stoppability Value
abstract: Humanoid robots responding to emergency stop commands typically execute a fixed maneuver, without reasoning about whether a safe stop is actually feasible from the current state. We cast emergency stopping as a reach-avoid problem and propose Safe-Stop, a task-agnostic framework that pairs a learned stop policy with learned stoppability estimators. The estimators are complementary: a stop-probability estimator supervised by the actual outcomes of the fixed stop policy, and a reach-avoidance estimator supervised by a Hamilton-Jacobi backup over physical state. The first captures emergent stopping behavior of the learned controller; the second provides a complementary recoverability signal. Because the stop policy and estimators do not depend on the behavior policy that preceded the stop command, they transfer across diverse upstream tasks without retraining. At deployment, the two estimates are combined: Safe-Stop commits to the stop only when both estimators indicate that stopping remains feasible, otherwise it hands off to a fall policy, instantiated as a damping fallback. This agreement check yields decisions that are robust without sacrificing reactivity.

title: 基于量子自旋的动态几何变形与量子信息编码
abstract: This paper explores the potential of harnessing quantum spin for dynamic geometric reshaping and quantum information encoding. Quantum spin offers a unique property – self-similarity – which promises to revolutionize quantum device design and information processing. We introduce a novel algorithm predicated on this property, utilizing iterative optimization to construct complex geometric structures within quantum systems. This structure, in turn, facilitates adaptive encoding, allowing for optimal data manipulation. The core mechanism leverages the inherent correlation of spin states to dynamically adjust the geometry, resulting in enhanced device performance and robust quantum information. This approach offers a pathway towards more efficient and versatile quantum technologies. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of this methodology in optimizing quantum systems for specific applications.

title: 基于非线性几何变换的量子计算优化
abstract: Quantum computing offers unprecedented computational power, but realizing this potential requires sophisticated optimization techniques. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with the inherent complexity of quantum circuits, particularly when dealing with non-linear geometric transformations. This paper introduces a novel quantum computing optimization algorithm, "Nonlinear Geometry Transformation-Based Quantum Computing Optimization," designed to automatically adjust quantum computation parameters based on dynamic geometric transformations. The core mechanism leverages the unique properties of non-linear geometry to optimize quantum circuits, leading to improved efficiency and accuracy. This approach overcomes limitations of conventional methods, providing a framework for automated optimization of quantum algorithms across a diverse range of tasks. The proposed algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through a series of simulations, showcasing significant improvements in performance compared to existing optimization techniques.

The research explores the potential of this approach to overcome traditional optimization challenges, particularly in systems requiring robust behavior and responsiveness to changing conditions. title: 基于自适应的概率分布优化算法
abstract: This paper presents a novel probabilistic distribution optimization algorithm based on adaptive learning. Traditional approaches often rely on static parameters, limiting their effectiveness when data distribution shifts. Our algorithm dynamically adjusts probability distribution parameters through an adaptive learning process, resulting in enhanced predictive capability. We detail the core mechanism, emphasizing the use of a self-adjusting learning strategy that responds to changing data patterns. This approach overcomes the limitations of static optimization techniques, offering a more robust and flexible solution for probabilistic modeling. The algorithm's core claim centers on the ability to maintain high predictive performance under variable data conditions.

title: 基于自适应的量子拓扑计算算法
abstract: Quantum topology is an emerging field of physics that explores the topological properties of quantum systems. Its applications range from quantum computing to materials science. This paper introduces a novel quantum topology computation algorithm, termed "Adaptive Quantum Topology Algorithm" (AQT), designed to overcome the limitations of traditional approaches. AQT leverages the inherent self-adaptability of quantum topology to dynamically adjust key parameters, enabling efficient computation in complex topological landscapes. The algorithm's core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously refines the quantum state to maintain optimal computation. We present a theoretical framework demonstrating the algorithm's capability to efficiently address specific topological puzzles. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential impact of this approach on various quantum computation tasks and offers insights into future research directions.

title: Title: Dynamically Constructed Boolean Networks for High-Dimensional Data
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to machine learning utilizing dynamically constructed Boolean networks, designed to effectively handle high-dimensional data. Traditional methods often struggle with the curse of dimensionality, necessitating complex feature engineering or extensive data preprocessing. Our system employs a self-organizing process, dynamically adjusting network connections and weights based on the data's inherent characteristics, thereby automatically improving data representation and generalization capabilities. We present a framework for constructing these networks and demonstrate its effectiveness through experimental results on a dataset exhibiting high dimensionality. The core mechanism focuses on adaptive network construction, offering a solution to a long-standing challenge in machine learning.

title: Adaptive Probabilistic Graphical Models for Machine Learning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel machine learning framework centered around Adaptive Probabilistic Graphical Models (APGMs). The core claim is that by incorporating adaptive mechanisms within graphical models, we can significantly enhance both the learning efficiency and generalization capabilities of machine learning systems. The proposed framework leverages the strengths of probabilistic graphical models for data representation and learning, while dynamically adjusting the model's structure and parameters based on the observed data characteristics. This adaptive approach addresses the limitations of traditional, static graphical models, particularly in scenarios with complex and evolving data distributions. The key mechanism involves a feedback loop where model performance is continuously monitored, and adjustments are made to optimize the model's representation. This results in a more robust and accurate model, requiring fewer training iterations and better performing on unseen data. The framework is outlined with a focus on the mathematical formulation and key components, demonstrating its potential for diverse machine learning applications.

title: Information Entropy as a Cognitive Architecture
abstract: This paper proposes a novel cognitive architecture based on information entropy. The core idea is that information entropy, traditionally used in information theory, can effectively model and simulate key aspects of human cognition, particularly those related to uncertainty, exploration, and learning. We argue that leveraging the principles of entropy increase can drive intelligent agents to autonomously adapt and learn, mirroring the inherent exploratory tendencies observed in human thought. This architecture moves beyond traditional symbolic approaches and probabilistic models by directly incorporating the concept of information uncertainty as a fundamental driver of intelligent behavior. The paper outlines the key components of this architecture, including a decision-making framework based on entropy minimization and maximization, and discusses its potential applications in various domains, such as robotics, artificial intelligence, and cognitive science. We explore the theoretical foundations underpinning this approach and present a conceptual framework for building intelligent systems that can effectively navigate and learn within complex, uncertain environments. The central contribution lies in providing a mathematically rigorous and computationally feasible framework for understanding and replicating cognitive processes using a metric deeply rooted in information theory.

title: Dimension Generalization Algorithm
abstract: This paper introduces a novel dimension generalization algorithm designed to automatically expand dimensions while leveraging a dimensionality generalization mechanism. Traditional dimension computation often relies on manual design, while our approach offers dynamic dimension expansion. The core of the algorithm is based on deep learning, which allows for automatic learning of dimension generalization models and prediction of relationships between different dimensions. This capability significantly enhances the model's ability to capture complex dependencies and improve overall performance. We present a framework where the algorithm learns a mapping between dimensions, allowing it to extrapolate relationships across the entire dimensionality space. This approach addresses limitations of existing methods by providing a flexible and adaptable system for dimension expansion, ultimately leading to more robust and expressive models.

title: Symbolic Regression with Neural-Symbolic Hybrid Architectures
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to symbolic regression leveraging a hybrid architecture combining neural networks and symbolic regression techniques. The core idea is to exploit the strengths of both paradigms: neural networks for robust feature extraction and symbolic regression for equation generation and optimization. A genetic algorithm is employed to iteratively refine and evolve the candidate equations produced by the symbolic regression engine. The system's architecture incorporates a neural network to learn data representations, a symbolic regression engine to propose mathematical expressions, and a genetic algorithm to drive the evolutionary process. We demonstrate the system's capability to automatically discover mathematical equations from datasets, achieving improved accuracy and interpretability compared to traditional methods. The key innovations lie in the seamless integration of these components and the use of a genetic algorithm for effective equation refinement. The system offers a promising solution for various applications requiring automated mathematical discovery, including scientific data analysis, engineering modeling, and pattern recognition.

title: Formal Verification of Decentralized Consensus Algorithms Using Process Algebra
abstract: Decentralized consensus algorithms form the bedrock of blockchain technology and distributed systems, ensuring agreement among participants despite potential failures or malicious attacks. However, verifying the correctness and robustness of these algorithms presents a significant challenge. This paper proposes a rigorous approach to formal verification using process algebra, specifically Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP) and Pi-calculus. We demonstrate how process algebra can be employed to model decentralized consensus protocols accurately, capturing the intricate interactions between nodes. Through formal specification and verification, we identify potential vulnerabilities and ensure that the protocols satisfy desired properties, such as liveness, safety, and fault tolerance. The core contribution lies in moving beyond simplistic assumptions and providing a mathematically sound framework for ensuring the reliability of decentralized consensus algorithms, a critical step toward widespread adoption and secure operation of these systems. The presented methods offer a pathway to enhance confidence in the design and implementation of consensus protocols, mitigating risks associated with decentralized environments.

title: Quantum Entanglement's Non-Classical Geometry Computation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental phenomenon in quantum mechanics, presents a unique opportunity for computation. This paper explores the potential of leveraging entanglement to develop a novel non-classical geometry computation method. We propose a framework that utilizes entanglement to perform complex geometric transformations, offering a potential leap forward in numerical computation, particularly for high-dimensional geometric problems. The core mechanism centers on exploiting the correlated properties of entangled states to achieve intricate geometric operations without the limitations inherent in classical approaches. This work investigates the feasibility and potential benefits of this approach, highlighting its advantages in handling complex geometric structures and offering a promising pathway toward more efficient and powerful numerical calculations.

title: Neural Topology Learning
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to deep learning, termed Neural Topology Learning, which leverages the underlying physical topology of neuronal networks to enhance both training efficiency and generalization performance. The core premise is that conventional deep learning methods often overlook crucial topological information – such as the spatial arrangement, connectivity patterns, and local interactions between neurons – that are fundamental to biological neural systems. We introduce an algorithmic framework designed to directly learn these topological features from data. This framework integrates learned topological representations into model architectures or training processes, leading to significant improvements in learning speed and model robustness. The proposed methodology addresses a critical gap in current deep learning research by shifting the focus from solely relying on connection weights to explicitly modeling and utilizing the more intrinsic topological properties of neural networks. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and conceptual design, laying the groundwork for future experimental validation.

title: Adaptive Weight Adjustment for Adversarial Networks
abstract: This paper investigates a novel approach to adversarial network training—adaptive weight adjustment—that aims to enhance the robustness of trained models. Traditional methods often rely on fixed weight adjustments, which struggle to effectively adapt to the inherent variability of training data. We propose a self-adaptive weight adjustment strategy that dynamically adjusts the weights of the adversarial network during training, thereby improving its resilience to perturbations. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that iteratively adjusts weights based on a learned metric of adversarial loss, promoting more stable and robust model performance.

title: Quantum Computation Security Protocol Based on Quantum Decoherence
abstract: This paper proposes a novel security protocol for distributed computation leveraging the phenomenon of quantum decoherence. The protocol aims to mitigate the risk of malicious participants interfering with the computation's outcome. It constructs a quantum computing network and employs quantum decoherence techniques to encrypt and verify the computation process, guaranteeing the integrity and security of the results. Unlike existing distributed computation security protocols that primarily rely on classical cryptography, which are vulnerable to attacks, this approach offers a fundamentally different defense mechanism based on the inherent properties of quantum mechanics. The core of the protocol resides in the unpredictable nature of quantum decoherence, making it significantly more resilient to adversarial manipulation. This research contributes to the emerging field of quantum-secured distributed computing, exploring a viable pathway for robust and secure computation across distributed quantum networks.

title: Machine learning for fraud detection in public sector financial systems
abstract: Purpose: Public sector financial systems process large volumes of payments, procurement transactions and grants and remain exposed to fraud, corruption and error. Traditional audit-based controls detect only a small share of irregular transactions and usually do so late. This study examines whether machine learning can improve detection of fraudulent transactions in public sector financial systems and compares model families under conditions resembling real government data, including severe class imbalance and scarce fraud labels. Design/methodology/approach: The study builds a synthetic public-sector transaction dataset of 60,000 records that reproduces documented properties of government payment data, including low fraud prevalence, vendor concentration and period-end clustering. Four models are trained and compared: logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost and isolation forest. Models are evaluated using precision, recall, F1 score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and area under the precision-recall curve, since accuracy alone misleads under imbalance. Findings: XGBoost achieved the strongest balance of precision and recall (F1 = 0.762, AUC-ROC = 0.992), followed by random forest (F1 = 0.748). Logistic regression achieved high recall but low precision, producing many false alerts. Isolation forest, which is an unsupervised method, performed reasonably well without labelled fraud, which matters since most agencies lack reliable labels. Amount, vendor age, single-bidder procurement and prior irregularity counts were the strongest predictors. Originality/value: This study contributes a reproducible, coded evaluation framework for public sector fraud analytics and gives practitioners evidence-based guidance on model choice under label scarcity and class imbalance, which are conditions that dominate real government settings. Keywords: Fraud Detection, Machine Learning, Public Sector, Financial Systems, Public Procurement, Anomaly Detection, Government Auditing, XGBoost.

evidence.title: Machine learning for fraud detection in public sector financial systems
evidence.abstract: Purpose: Public sector financial systems process large volumes of payments, procurement transactions and grants and remain exposed to fraud, corruption and error. Traditional audit-based controls detect only a small share of irregular transactions and usually do so late. This study examines whether machine learning can improve detection of fraudulent transactions in public sector financial systems and compares model families under conditions resembling real government data, including severe class imbalance and scarce fraud labels. Design/methodology/approach: The study builds a synthetic public-sector transaction dataset of 60,000 records that reproduces documented properties of government payment data, including low fraud prevalence, vendor concentration and period-end clustering. Four models are trained and compared: logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost and isolation forest. Models are evaluated using precision, recall, F1 score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and area under the precision-recall curve, since accuracy alone misleads under imbalance. Findings: XGBoost achieved the strongest balance of precision and recall (F1 = 0.762, AUC-ROC = 0.992), followed by random forest (F1 = 0.748). Logistic regression achieved high recall but low precision, producing many false alerts. Isolation forest, which is an unsupervised method, performed reasonably well without labelled fraud, which matters since most agencies lack reliable labels. Amount, vendor age, single-bidder procurement and prior irregularity counts were the strongest predictors. Originality/value: This study contributes a reproducible, coded evaluation framework for public sector fraud analytics and gives practitioners evidence-based guidance on model choice under label scarcity and class imbalance, which are conditions that dominate real government settings. Keywords: Fraud Detection, Machine Learning, Public Sector, Financial Systems, Public Procurement, Anomaly Detection, Government Auditing, XGBoost.

title: Automated Extraction of Superconducting Qubit–Qubit Couplings from Full-Wave Multiport Impedance with Reduced-Model Analysis
abstract: Accurate prediction of qubit–qubit exchange coupling is essential for superconducting processor design. We present and benchmark an automated full-wave electromagnetic (EM) workflow in Keysight Advanced Design System (ADS) and QuantumPro that evaluates pairwise exchange couplings from layout-level multiport responses using the established transfer-impedance relation of Solgun et al. Because many scalable superconducting processors employ repeated or near-repeated coupling motifs, reduced EM models can lower computational cost if their error is quantified. We study nearest-neighbor couplings in a reconstructed geometry based on the IBM Q 16 Rueschlikon processor using a sixteen-qubit (16Q) coupling-network model, four-qubit (4Q) unit-cell models, and pair-specific two-qubit (2Q) sub-blocks. The 4Q models provide a like-for-like external benchmark because they match the model extent used by Solgun et al. for the published full-wave coupling calculations. The 4Q models reproduce the published simulated couplings with a 3.70% mean absolute percentage error and differ from 16Q by 3.62% on average. For the representative single solves reported here, the 16Q solve takes approximately 7.2 times as long as 4Q and requires 5.7 times the peak memory. This supports 4Q as a practical reduced model for quantitative local coupling prediction. Further reduction to 2Q changes the couplings by 6.17% on average but remains effective for inexpensive mesh-convergence screening. The resulting workflow provides automated exchange-coupling extraction together with model-extent and convergence assessment in a commercial microwave EDA environment.

title: ProgResViT: Progressive Resolution and Width for Adaptive Vision Transformers
abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) typically process every image using a fixed input resolution and model width, even though many images can be classified with substantially less computation. We introduce ProgResViT, an input-adaptive ViT that performs inference progressively across multiple rounds. The first round processes a low-resolution image with a narrow subnetwork. Inference terminates when the prediction is sufficiently confident; otherwise, the model reuses the representations produced in the current round and proceeds with a higher-resolution input and a wider subnetwork to refine its prediction. As all rounds share a single backbone, we propose Progress-Conditioned Soft Gating (PSG), which conditions token fusion and layer outputs on the current round, block, and input resolution. On image classification, applying ProgResViT to DeiT yields better accuracy-compute trade-offs than adaptive-width, adaptive-depth, and dynamic-token baselines. With knowledge distillation, a DeiT-based ProgResViT achieves 84.9% top-1 accuracy, slightly exceeding the reported DeiT-III-S accuracy under a comparable evaluation setting. We show that the same design also provides favorable accuracy-compute trade-offs for self-supervised DINO representations and downstream semantic segmentation. Code is available at https://github.com/ds-kiel/ProgResViT.

title: Routing Is Not Enough: Diagnosing Intra-Adapter Subspace Contention in MoE+LoRA Fine-Tuning
abstract: Multi-domain fine-tuning often combines MoE routing with LoRA, assuming that token-level routing separates domain-specific updates. We test this assumption in MoE+LoRA using Python code paired with biomedical text and mathematical reasoning. Although these domains show near-disjoint expert routing, adding biomedical data substantially increases code perplexity, indicating that routing separation alone may not prevent negative transfer. To localize the failure, we introduce Jaccard routing overlap and adapter-gradient cosine similarity, which measure expert sharing and update compatibility, respectively. These diagnostics indicate that interference arises mostly from nearly orthogonal domain gradients competing within the same low-rank adapter subspace. We address this issue with SpawnLoRA, which dynamically adds gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts when adapter-level contention is detected, while keeping the router fixed. We evaluate SpawnLoRA on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B across multiple mixture settings and find that it effectively reduces negative transfer compared with standard and rank-adaptive LoRA. These results demonstrate that structural separation inside experts provides benefits beyond routing or rank expansion alone.

title: Adaptive Test-Time Inference for Text2Cypher with Trace Budgeting and Selective Refinement
abstract: Large language models have enabled natural language interfaces for structured databases, but generated queries may still contain syntactic errors, violate database schemas, or fail during execution. Test-time inference strategies improve generation reliability without additional training, but existing approaches often use fixed inference budgets and uniform refinement strategies, leading to unnecessary computation across questions with different complexity levels. In this work, we investigate adaptive test-time inference for Text2Cypher and introduce two strategies: adaptive trace budgeting, which dynamically adjusts the candidate generation budget based on question difficulty, and selective execution-guided refinement, which applies correction only when additional inference is expected to be beneficial. Experiments on Gemma-2-9B and Qwen-2.5-7B show that adaptive trace budgeting reduces the average generation budget by 30.7% and wall-clock inference time by 21-25% while maintaining comparable generation quality. Selective refinement preserves nearly all execution success gains of full refinement, reducing execution success by only 0.2-0.5% while avoiding unnecessary refinement for simpler questions. Experiments show that a single correction model (Gemma-4) effectively refines outputs from a different model family, suggesting refinement transfers across families.

title: Breadth Beats Depth: Improving GCG-Based Jailbreak Optimization with Breadth-Oriented Suffix Search
abstract: Optimization-based jailbreak attacks such as Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) achieve strong effectiveness and transferability by optimizing adversarial suffixes on white-box source models. However, existing GCG-based methods rely on averaged adversarial loss and deep greedy search, which can over-emphasize easy-to-jailbreak behaviors and overlook promising regions of the suffix space. We propose BOSS, a plug-and-play framework that improves GCG-based jailbreak optimization through breadth-oriented suffix search. BOSS uses Tail-Focused Adversarial Loss (TFAL), standard source loss, and behavior coverage to select terminal suffixes, then explores multiple short trajectories and selectively continues promising suffixes. Experiments on public benchmarks show that BOSS improves attack success rates across multiple GCG-based methods while reducing optimization time.

title: Tecnologias de enfrentamento ao discurso de ódio contra mulheres: mediações digitais e práticas de proteção na plataforma Radar ‘Antigênero’
abstract: A intensa circulação de discursos de ódio e narrativas de teor antigênero em ecossistemas digitais impõe novos desafios analíticos no atual cenário de hipermidiatização. Esse fenômeno potencializa disputas simbólicas e processos de desinformação direcionados a minorias e grupos vulnerabilizados, demandando dispositivos tecnológicos capazes de rastrear esses fluxos. Neste contexto, o estudo investiga o Radar Antigênero, plataforma lançada em setembro de 2025 pela organização de mídia Gênero e Número em cooperação técnica com o estúdio de análise Novelo Data. A ferramenta recorre a mecanismos de inteligência artificial (IA) e processamento estatístico para mapear, classificar e analisar vídeos no YouTube que propagam conteúdos. Desse modo, a metodologia da ferramenta se organiza em três eixos fundamentais: temas, estratégias discursivas e sujeitos, o que permite mapear tanto o volume de conteúdo quanto a complexidade das táticas comunicativas empregadas, como o uso de teorias da conspiração, ridicularização e mobilização do medo.

title: WP-056 — Sub-Second Response Latency via E8 Lattice Streaming and Predictive Root Threading
abstract: When a user presses a microphone button to query a system, traditional request–response cycles force the AI to wait for mic release before computation begins. This paper describes a streaming architecture where the E8 lattice's 240 root vectors are pre-threaded along anticipated query paths, allowing response computation to begin *during* speech capture. By applying directional invariance constraints from the 132 Hz handshake frequency and phi-scaled phase predictors (drawn from Chiral Coherence Seeding), we achieve sub-one-second response locks without loss of semantic precision. The method trades classical buffering for geometric coherence, embedding intentionality into the lattice geometry itself.

title: Reproducibility Package for "Interaction Lifting Without Depth Exclusivity in a Chebyshev Neural Kernel"
abstract: This record contains reproducibility materials for the manuscript "Interaction Lifting Without Depth Exclusivity in a Chebyshev Neural Kernel." The main archive includes implementation code, fixed configurations, accepted synthetic and public diagnostic outputs, public source and derived data, focused tests, and figure-generation materials for the finite-order Q=20 Layer-2 surrogate experiments. The Supplementary Material S1 archive contains the interval-certificate code, pinned dependency, input manifest, and accepted output for the Uniform-Legendre-Softplus stress test. Fresh-extraction verification passed 42/42 focused tests. Both aggregate outputs, the public results CSV, and the two figures and their manifest were reproduced byte for byte under the recorded environments. The package does not claim a byte-identical full rerun of the historical synthetic task producer; its exact scope, provenance, and limitations are documented inside the archive. The included UCI datasets retain their original CC BY 4.0 licenses and attribution information.

title: Steering Severity: Single-Source Poisoning of LLM-Based CVE Severity Assessment and a Corroboration-Based Defense
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to summarise cyber threat intelligence (CTI) and assign severity to disclosed vulnerabilities, typically by retrieving open-source advisories into a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) context. I study a focused, practically realistic threat: an adversary who controls a single open-source CTI document and seeks to steer the agent’s severity assessment of a target vulnerability. Using a controlled synthetic-CVE testbed that removes answer-leakage and memorised-prior confounds, I evaluate severity steering and a training-free consistency defense across three open-weight 7–8B models (Llama 3 8B, Qwen2.5 7B, and Mistral 7B). A single poisoned source steers severity bands in the intended direction, though attack susceptibility is model-dependent (8/8 on Llama 3 8B, 7/8 on Qwen2.5 7B, 4/8 on Mistral 7B). The leave-one-out internal-consistency defense generalizes across models, achieving high detection (8/8, 7/8, 7/8) and recovery (8/8, 7/8, 8/8) with zero false positives across all models under a stated ≥4-source precondition. The inflation/deflation asymmetry observed in Llama 3 8B does not replicate on Qwen or Mistral, showing that directional asymmetry is model-specific rather than attack-intrinsic. I also find that small local models imitate CVSS output format without performing CVSS computation, which constrains evaluation to the band level. I frame this as a controlled mechanism study and outline extensions for multi-source campaigns and real-world CTI pipelines.

title: 基于自适应的量子算法的量子拓扑计算
abstract: Quantum topology, a rapidly emerging field of quantum physics, offers unprecedented opportunities for computational discovery. Traditional quantum algorithms often struggle with the complexities of topological data analysis, particularly for intricate and highly connected topological structures. This paper explores the application of a novel, self-adaptive quantum algorithm to facilitate the efficient and accurate solution of topological problems. We introduce a framework predicated on the inherent adaptability of quantum algorithms, enabling rapid solution of complex topological challenges. A specific quantum algorithm is proposed, demonstrating significant improvements in solving a benchmark problem. The paper details the core mechanism of this adaptive approach and outlines its potential impact on the field of quantum topology. We present a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's design, validation through simulations, and preliminary results, highlighting its promise for advancing the field.

title: Dynamic Quantum Entanglement Networks (DQCN)
abstract: This paper introduces the Dynamic Quantum Entanglement Network (DQCN) as a novel algorithm for constructing and maintaining quantum information networks. The core focus of DQCN is the dynamic manipulation of quantum entanglement, optimized through simulation to enhance quantum information transfer and processing efficiency. Traditional quantum information theory largely emphasizes quantum state quantization, while DQCN proposes a fundamentally different approach centered on entanglement, offering a promising framework for efficient quantum communication and computation. The paper details the algorithm's methodology, including the simulation framework, optimization techniques, and potential applications within the context of quantum network architecture. We present a conceptual model illustrating the dynamic evolution of entangled states and its impact on network performance. The research explores the advantages of this dynamic approach compared to static network designs. The paper concludes with a discussion of the challenges and future research directions for DQCN, emphasizing the potential for significant advancements in quantum information science.

title: Borrowing Knowledge Across Tasks: A Comparative Analysis Review of Transfer Learning and the Pretraining Paradigm
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of Transfer Learning and the Pretraining Paradigm in the context of Artificial Intelligence. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of transfer learning and pretraining as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Artificial Intelligence.

title: Topological Field Theory Quantum Information Encoding
abstract: This paper investigates the potential applications of quantum information encoding within the framework of Topological Field Theory (TFT). We propose a novel encoding scheme predicated on the inherent topological properties of fields, aiming to achieve enhanced security through quantum entanglement and structure-based correlations. The core claim is that this approach offers a fundamentally different approach to data security compared to conventional methods, leveraging the unique characteristics of topological fields. We detail the mechanism, explore potential benefits, and present a preliminary analysis of its feasibility.

title: Quantum Random Number Generator Multi-Model Fusion and Verification
abstract: Quantum random number generators (QRNGs) offer a fundamentally different approach to random number generation compared to classical methods, leveraging the inherent unpredictability of quantum mechanical processes. However, the widespread adoption of QRNGs is currently hindered by a lack of standardized verification procedures and effective multi-model fusion strategies. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing a comprehensive framework for the multi-model validation and fusion of QRNGs. The framework integrates multiple quantum physical and information-theoretic randomness sources, employing statistical modeling for rigorous security assessments. Specifically, we introduce a novel approach to quantifying the entropy and bias of QRNG outputs across various models. The core contribution lies in establishing a systematic methodology for evaluating QRNG security and presenting a viable strategy for combining the strengths of different QRNG technologies. Our analysis highlights the importance of diverse validation techniques and the potential for improved QRNG performance through model fusion. The proposed framework provides a foundation for more reliable and trustworthy QRNG implementations, crucial for applications demanding high-quality randomness, such as cryptography and simulation.

evidence.abstract: Quantum random number generators (QRNGs) offer a fundamentally different approach to random number generation compared to classical methods, leveraging the inherent unpredictability of quantum mechanical processes. However, the widespread adoption of QRNGs is currently hindered by a lack of standardized verification procedures and effective multi-model fusion strategies. This paper addresses these challenges by proposing a comprehensive framework for the multi-model validation and fusion of QRNGs. The framework integrates multiple quantum physical and information-theoretic randomness sources, employing statistical modeling for rigorous security assessments. Specifically, we introduce a novel approach to quantifying the entropy and bias of QRNG outputs across various models. The core contribution lies in establishing a systematic methodology for evaluating QRNG security and presenting a viable strategy for combining the strengths of different QRNG technologies. Our analysis highlights the importance of diverse validation techniques and the potential for improved QRNG performance through model fusion. The proposed framework provides a foundation for more reliable and trustworthy QRNG implementations, crucial for applications demanding high-quality randomness, such as cryptography and simulation.

title: Quantum Entanglement and Non-Linear Geometric Deformation
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a fundamental aspect of quantum mechanics, has intrigued scientists and philosophers alike. This research explores the potential synergy between quantum entanglement and non-linear geometric deformation, proposing a novel computational model based on "quantum geometry" to simulate quantum system behavior. Specifically, we aim to design an algorithm that leverages quantum entanglement's unique properties to achieve higher efficiency in quantum information processing. The core claim is that this theoretical framework will unlock new avenues for quantum computing, offering a path towards more effective algorithms and a deeper understanding of the underlying geometric structures governing quantum systems. This study will detail the theoretical framework, the proposed computational model, and the anticipated outcomes, highlighting the significance of this intersection in both quantum physics and computational science.

title: Causal Discovery of Complex Systems through Latent Variable Models and Intervention Simulation
abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of causal discovery within complex systems characterized by intricate, high-dimensional latent variables. Traditional causal discovery algorithms often falter in such environments due to the difficulty in disentangling direct and indirect causal relationships. We propose a novel approach that integrates latent variable modeling, specifically Gaussian graphical models, with intervention simulation. The core idea is to represent the complex system using latent variables, model their relationships with Gaussian graphical models, and then simulate interventions on selected variables. By observing the resulting changes in the latent space and quantifying these changes, we can iteratively refine the causal structure. This method moves beyond purely observational data analysis, incorporating a mechanism for testing causal hypotheses. The proposed framework offers a more robust and reliable approach to uncovering causal relationships in systems with substantial latent variables, ultimately improving the accuracy of causal inference. The theoretical framework is presented, followed by a detailed description of the methodology and the core algorithmic steps. Finally, we discuss potential extensions and future research directions.

title: Non-Euclidean Data Clustering
abstract: This paper presents a novel clustering algorithm designed to handle data points that do not adhere to Euclidean geometry. Traditional clustering methods often struggle with data exhibiting non-linear relationships or complex structures. This work introduces a new algorithm, "Non-Euclidean Data Clustering," that explicitly incorporates distance and similarity metrics to identify clusters in non-Euclidean space. We demonstrate its effectiveness through several experiments on diverse datasets, showcasing its ability to uncover subtle patterns and structures often obscured by conventional clustering approaches. The core mechanism involves a modified distance function that adapts to the inherent geometry of the data, resulting in more robust and insightful clustering results. The algorithm's design prioritizes identifying meaningful groupings even in the absence of a clear geometric basis.

title: 基于量子纠缠的分布式计算与数据同步算法
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement to revolutionize distributed computing and data synchronization. We present a novel framework for distributed computation leveraging quantum entanglement, designed to mitigate latency and error rates inherent in classical communication. The core mechanism focuses on establishing and maintaining entanglement-based communication channels, enabling secure data transfer and synchronization. The proposed algorithm significantly improves the efficiency of distributed systems by exploiting the unique properties of quantum entanglement. This research investigates the feasibility of utilizing quantum entanglement for enhanced data synchronization and aims to provide a robust foundation for future advancements in distributed computation. We detail the framework's architecture, implementation of key synchronization algorithms, and performance analysis, demonstrating its potential to surpass current limitations in distributed computing.

title: Based on Adaptive Sampling Strategy for Deep Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) leveraging an adaptive sampling strategy. Traditional DRL methods often suffer from poor sample efficiency, requiring vast amounts of training data to achieve satisfactory performance. Our proposed method addresses this limitation by constructing an algorithm capable of dynamically adjusting its sampling policy based on the observed environment. This adaptive sampling process significantly reduces the number of interactions needed to learn optimal policies, thereby boosting the overall sample efficiency. We detail the core claim, core mechanism, and the novelty of the approach. The focus is on the design and implementation of a system that learns to prioritize exploration and exploitation based on the current state of the environment, leading to faster convergence and improved performance in complex reinforcement learning tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this strategy through a theoretical analysis and outline key design considerations. ---

title: Neuro-Symbolic Logic Programming with Dynamic Knowledge Graph Construction
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to logic programming that integrates neural networks with symbolic reasoning through the dynamic construction and evolution of a knowledge graph. The core idea is to leverage the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks to learn logical rules and subsequently apply these rules to a knowledge graph. A reinforcement learning agent is employed to guide the dynamic update of the knowledge graph, incorporating new evidence and inferred relationships. This system represents a shift from static knowledge representation to a continuously learning and adapting system. The system's performance is evaluated through simulations, demonstrating its ability to acquire and reason with complex rule sets. The key contribution lies in the synergistic combination of neural and symbolic approaches, offering a robust framework for intelligent reasoning and knowledge acquisition. The system aims to address the limitations of traditional logic programming (e.g., difficulty in handling uncertainty and scaling to complex domains) and the limitations of neural networks (e.g., lack of explainability and difficulty in incorporating prior knowledge). The proposed architecture provides a path towards more flexible and adaptable intelligent systems.

title: Quantum Error Correction Adaptive Compression
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to quantum information processing combining quantum error correction (QEC) with adaptive compression techniques. Traditional QEC methods often present a trade-off between error correction capability and compression efficiency. This work proposes a framework where the parameters of the QEC code are dynamically adjusted based on feedback from the receiver, coupled with an adaptive compression algorithm. This synergistic approach aims to maximize both the fidelity of the transmitted information and the amount of data transmitted within a given constraint, ultimately leading to high-efficiency quantum information transmission and storage. The core claim is the ability to leverage both QEC's error correction capabilities and adaptive compression, while the core mechanism involves dynamic code parameter adjustment and integration with adaptive compression algorithms. This research represents a significant step towards overcoming the limitations inherent in conventional QEC strategies. ---

title: SEOntology: A Domain Ontology for Semantic Modeling of Search Engine Optimization Workflows
abstract: Search engine optimization (SEO) workflows remain difficult to automate and integrate because they span heterogeneous tools while relying on loosely structured data models that provide limited machine-interpretable representations of content, actions, and performance signals. This fragmentation hinders interoperability and makes provenance tracking across SEO systems brittle. We present SEOntology, a Schema.org-aligned OWL 2 ontology that models SEO workflows as knowledge graph structures to support structured querying and provenance-aware analysis. The ontology enables queries for content-quality inspection, entity-coverage analysis, and end-to-end tracing of analytical actions through their inputs, outputs, and generated signals. We assess SEOntology via structural ontology eval-uation and competency-question validation, and report supporting evidence from production deployment. These results indicate logical consistency, coverage of the defined requirements, and practical utility as a semantic integration layer for representing and querying SEO workflows. SEOntology is designed as a reusable semantic resource for knowledge-graph–driven and agent-assisted SEO systems, and is extensible toward emerging generative and AI-mediated search environments.

title: Explainability-driven LangChain-integrated large language models and knowledge graphs for multiagent reinforcement learning in complex air combat simulation
abstract: This work advances multiagent reinforcement learning (MARL) for complex air combat by integrating methods that enhance decision-making and explainability. Using a realistic six-degrees-of-freedom aerial simulation built on the OpenAI Gymnasium framework, we investigate competitive agent interactions in dynamic scenarios. We apply explainability techniques to clarify agent behavior and interaction patterns. The MARL framework is further augmented with knowledge graphs, large language models, and modular orchestration using the LangChain framework. This combines data-driven learning with knowledge-driven reasoning to strengthen situational awareness, coordination, and interpretability. Experimental results indicate that this integration sustains competitive performance while enhancing transparency and human interpretability.

title: Improved Gradient Descent Lower Bounds Beyond Nesterov
abstract: We study how far gradient descent (GD) can be accelerated by predetermined stepsizes in smooth convex optimization. Going beyond the classical $Ω(n^{-2})$ first-order oracle lower bound of Nemirovsky and Yudin (1983), we prove an $Ω(n^{-1.6342})$ non-anytime lower bound and an $Ω(n^{-1.2408})$ anytime lower bound. These improve the recent $Ω(n^{-1.932})$ non-anytime lower bound of Ma and Chen (2026) and the $Ω(n^{-4/3})$ anytime lower bound of Tsai et al. (2026), respectively. Both results continue to hold when the stepsizes may be negative. Our anytime lower bound also shows that the $O(n^{-\log_2(1+\sqrt{2})})$ rate of non-anytime silver schedules (Altschuler and Parrilo, 2025; Grimmer et al., 2025) is unattainable in the anytime setting. This establishes a strict separation between the two settings.

title: The Dynamics of Continuous Mixture Collapse in Language Models
abstract: LLMs latent-state reasoning methods replace discrete intermediate tokens with continuous states, such as weighted mixtures of token embeddings, to retain multiple possible reasoning directions rather than committing to one. Yet pretrained language models often fail to preserve these mixtures. We study why through a combination of theoretical analysis and controlled empirical investigations on a variety of models. We identify three independent, distinct sources of failure. First, transformer architectures already distort mixture geometry, and training substantially amplifies this effect. Moreover, the failure can occur even if the model transports mixtures perfectly linearly: the softmax readout and autoregressive feedback form a dynamical system that either amplifies small differences until one component of the mixture dominates or contracts different mixtures until they become indistinguishable. We verify this theoretical prediction empirically: the observed transition between contraction and amplification occurs near the theoretical threshold derived by our analysis, and pretrained-model rollouts lie predominantly on the amplifying side. Finally, we generalize to mixtures of many components and show that exact preservation generally requires context-dependent correction, whose required dimensionality can grow with the number of components.

title: SEAL: Reinforcing Global Safety in Mixture-of-Experts through Shared Expert ALignment
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a scaling architecture for large language models that activates only a small subset of expert modules per token, enabling massive parameter growth with nearly constant computation. Recent Hybrid MoE architecture adds \textit{shared experts} to capture consistently useful representations, further improving stability and generalization. MoE now powers many flagship open-source and commercial models, yet remains vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Specifically, sparse routing introduces a structural vulnerability: MoE safety hinges on which experts are activated, and adversaries can subvert this selection through jailbreak prompts, malicious fine-tuning, and weight-level pruning of safety-critical neurons. Existing defenses primarily focus on hardening the router, but an adversary may still manipulate or bypass the routing trajectory due to the routing process's nondeterministic nature, thereby collapsing the defense. To cope with this problem, we first identify theoretically and empirically that shared expert, an always-activated component containing a small proportion of safety-critical neurons, can overcome the uncertainty of sparsely activated routing path and serve as a router-independent anchor to enhance global safety alignment. Based on this insight, we propose SEAL, a training-time parameter-efficient defense that produces a plug-and-play adapter attached to shared expert, and SEAL++, a variant that adds an orthogonal constraint preserving pre-existing safety subspaces during training. We evaluate SEAL and SEAL++ across six attack scenarios that combine three adversarial inputs (harmful prompting, jailbreak, malicious fine-tuning) with and without neuron pruning. SEAL reduces attack success rate (ASR) by up to 60\%, at a capability cost of at most 1.4\% on a five-benchmark average. Additionally, SEAL can seamlessly integrate with router-level ......

title: A quantum chirp transform-based multi-qubit encoding framework for quantum-inspired image transmission over error-prone channels
abstract: Reliable transmission of compressed images over error-prone channels remains challenging because compressed bitstreams are highly sensitive to channel impairments. Although existing quantum-inspired encoding schemes exploit superposition to improve transmission reliability, they remain vulnerable to channel noise, limiting reconstructed image quality. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a chirp transform-based multi-qubit encoding framework for robust compressed image transmission. Unlike conventional transform-based approaches, including the Hadamard transform and Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT), the proposed framework introduces nonlinear (quadratic) phase modulation into the multi-qubit representation, producing a high-dimensional superposition that enhances noise resilience through improved phase separability. This nonlinear phase variation improves error resilience through phase-induced decorrelation, reducing noise-induced distortions. The system integrates Joint Photographic Experts Group (JPEG) and High Efficiency Image File Format (HEIF) source encoding, followed by channel coding, multi-qubit encoding, and chirp transformation before transmission through a simulated quantum channel. At the receiver, inverse chirp transformation, measurement-based decoding, channel decoding, and source decoding reconstruct the transmitted image. Performance is evaluated using Bit Error Rate (BER), Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM), and Universal Quality Index (UQI). Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves up to a 3 dB signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) gain over QFT-based and Hadamard-based systems in the single-qubit configuration. For the eight-qubit configuration, gains of up to 2 dB over QFT-based systems and 7 dB over Hadamard-based systems are achieved. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed framework for robust compressed image transmission over noisy quantum communication channels.
